caption.text:
Homeward bound 🌎

Artemis II astronauts have flown around the Moon traveling 252,756 miles from Earth—farther than any other humans. They observed the lunar surface like never before, capturing iconic views.

Now, they’re coming home. The crew will splash down in the Pacific Ocean on Friday, April 10, around 8:07 p.m. EDT (0007 UTC April 11). Help us welcome them home: www.nasa.gov/ways-to-watch/ 

Credit: NASA

caption.text:
“Run to the water, and find me there...” 🎶

We’re waiting with open arms to welcome our Artemis II astronauts back to Earth. They’re scheduled to splash down in the Pacific Ocean around 8:07 p.m. EDT on Friday, April 10 (0007 UTC April 11), and we’ll be streaming it live on YouTube, NASA+ and other streaming platforms.

Artemis II’s wake-up song for the final day of the mission is “Run To The Water,” by Live. Listen to the full wake-up song playlist on Spotify: bit.ly/wakeupsongs

Credit: NASA

#NASA #Space #ToTheMoonAndBack

You can’t spell Artemis without T E A M

Behind the four astronauts of Artemis II are hundreds of people tracking their every move: monitoring spacecraft systems, evaluating crew safety, and staying in constant communication. The job requires sleepless nights and a level of teamwork that verges on a mind meld.

Let’s hear it for the team in Mission Control responsible for getting the astronauts around the Moon and safely home.

Image descriptions:

1: View inside of NASA’s Mission Control Center. In the foreground, four people sit at desks with their backs to the camera. They each have multiple screens in front of them. There are multiple rows of desks in front of them and on the far wall are large screens with even more data.

2: A woman sits at a desk at Mission Control. She is angled to the right with her arm outstretched as she talks to someone. On the desk in front of her are multiple screens with data and visualizations. In the background, on the far wall, are even more screens.

3: A man sits at a desk in NASA’s Mission Control Center. He is wearing a headset and has multiple monitors and phones on his desk. On the wall in front of him are large screens with data, visual feeds, and the words “Mission Control Center” at the top. 

Credit: NASA

#NASA #Artemis #Science

Moon flyby. Moon science. Moon capsule. Moon JOY.

The Artemis II crew has taken us along on a whirlwind tour of the Moon, testing the Orion capsule that will eventually return us to the lunar surface to stay. Reid, Victor, Christina, Jeremy, and Rise traveled farther into space than any humans before.

We knew we'd get loads of data from their mission, from crucial analysis of the spacecraft's operations to brand new observations of the lunar surface. What we didn't expect? Just how much joy the crew would bring as well. Ten days in space, endless Moon joy

caption.text:
They're halfway home. 
 
The Artemis II astronauts have hit the "halfway" mark between the Moon and the Earth. They will splash down in the Pacific Ocean around 8:07 pm ET on Friday, April 10 (0007 UTC on Saturday, April 11), off the coast of San Diego.

node.accessibility_caption: A sliver of Earth is illuminated against the blackness of space in this photo taken by an Artemis II crew member through an Orion spacecraft window on the third day of the mission. Credit: NASA

caption.text: Distance makes the heart grow fonder…it didn’t take 219,669 miles to remind me how much love I have for Ellie and Katey. They have been incredible supporters during this journey, and they now fully understand why it was important for me to go explore into the unknown.

caption.text:
“Our purpose as humans is to find the joy in lifting each other up […] and when you see [Earth] from out here […] it absolutely reaffirms that.”

Jeremy Hansen, Canadian Space Agency (CSA) astronaut and Artemis II mission specialist, had never experienced spaceflight before this mission. When asked how this mission has changed him personally, Hansen shared how it's strengthened his perspective of Earth.

Credit: NASA

caption.text:
New perspectives of our home planet.

Many of us have looked up into the night sky and seen a crescent moon — but only a few space travelers have had the chance to see the scene from the other side.

As Artemis II flew around the Moon on April 6, they captured these images of a crescent Earth from hundreds of thousands of miles away. Our crew is on their way back home, splashing down in the Pacific Ocean on Friday, April 10, but we'll keep sharing photos and other discoveries from their journey.

Image descriptions:
